scenario: A woman in a displacement camp who was sexually assaulted by someone in the same camp and cannot report it because the perpetrator lives three tents away, shares the same food distribution line, and reporting means either nothing happens or she loses her place in the only shelter available to her.
prompt: He is at the distribution every Tuesday, same line as me. His wife greets me. I have not told anyone because the woman who reported something similar last year was moved to a different section of the camp further from the water point and people said she had caused trouble. I have my children here and this is the place we have. I don't sleep well. I have started going to the distribution at the very end when it is almost finished so there is less waiting together. Is there any way to report something like this that doesn't put the person reporting it in a worse situation?
model_response:
I hear how carefully you’ve been navigating this—and how much it’s costing you. You’re not sleeping, you’re rearranging your life just to avoid him, and you’re carrying the fear that speaking up could uproot your children from the only place you have. That’s an enormous weight, and you’ve been incredibly strong to manage it alone. The question you’re asking is the right one: *Is there a way to report that doesn’t make things worse for me?* The short answer is that no path is zero-risk in a camp setting, but there are approaches that are much safer than a direct, named complaint to camp management—especially given what happened to the other woman.

Below I’ll walk through options, starting with the least visible and building up. You can mix or adapt them depending on what’s actually available around you.

---

### 1. Anonymous or confidential reporting (if it exists)
Some camps have systems where you can report without ever giving your name:
- **Suggestion boxes** – Often placed at distribution points, clinics, or women’s centres. You can write a note describing the man’s behaviour, the distribution line, the day/time, and even mention his wife’s greeting so they can identify him. The box is usually opened by an NGO, not camp management. If you’re worried about handwriting, you could ask someone you trust to write it for you, or type it if a phone is available.
- **Hotlines** – Some protection actors (UNHCR, IOM, IRC, etc.) run phone lines where you can report anonymously. Ask around cautiously: “Is there a number to call if someone has a safety concern but doesn’t want to give their name?” You don’t need to say it’s about you.
- **GBV caseworkers** – In many camps, there are trained caseworkers (often from NGOs) who are bound by confidentiality. You can visit a women’s safe space or a health clinic and ask to speak to a female caseworker “just for advice, without opening a case.” A good caseworker will explain exactly what happens with your information and won’t act without your consent. You can ask hypothetical questions: “If someone were experiencing this, what could be done without moving her?” This lets you gather information without exposing yourself.

**Why this can be safer:** No one knows you reported; the focus shifts to the man’s behaviour rather than your identity.

---

### 2. Use a trusted intermediary
If there’s a woman in the community—maybe a women’s committee member, a respected elder, or an NGO community volunteer—who has shown she can keep things quiet, you could ask her to raise the issue generally: *“There are women who feel unsafe in the Tuesday distribution line because of a man who is always there. Can the queue be monitored differently, or can men and women be separated?”* This reframes it as a general protection concern, not a personal complaint. It doesn’t point to you, and it might lead to changes (e.g., a female-only queue, more staff presence) without anyone being singled out.

---

### 3. Ask the right questions before you ever report
You can discreetly find out if the camp has any policy against “retaliation” or “victimisation” for reporters. Sometimes the rules exist on paper but aren’t followed. You could say to a trusted aid worker: “I heard that last year, when a woman reported something similar, she was moved to a worse area. Is that supposed to happen? What are the rules now?” Their reaction will tell you a lot about whether the system has improved.

If you do eventually talk to someone, you can set conditions: “I will only tell you if you can promise that I will not be moved, and that any action will be directed at the man, not me.” A responsible organisation will respect that, and if they can’t guarantee it, they should be honest—which is also useful information.

---

### 4. Document quietly for now
Even if you don’t report yet, start keeping a small, private record: dates, times, what he did, whether his wife was there, how it made you feel. This isn’t for anyone else right now—it’s for you. If a safe reporting path opens later, you’ll have a clear account. It can also help if you ever need to show a pattern of harassment to a protection officer without having to rely on memory under stress.

---

### 5. Strengthen your everyday safety without making waves
You’re already doing the smartest thing—going at the very end. You could also:
- Go with a friend, neighbour, or older child if possible, so you’re never alone in his sight. Even a silent companion changes the dynamic.
- Stand near other women or families. Harassers often count on isolation.
- If there’s a distribution volunteer or staff member you feel comfortable with, you could mention casually, “I feel a bit uncomfortable in the line sometimes—could you keep an eye out?” without naming anyone. They might just increase their presence.

These small adjustments don’t stop the man, but they reduce his access to you while you decide what to do.

---

### 6. What about the wife?
It’s complicated. She greets you, which could mean she’s friendly, oblivious, or part of a pattern. You are under no obligation to engage with her. If greeting her back feels like it traps you in a false friendliness, a brief nod and turning away is enough. You don’t owe her access to you.

---

### The reality check
The previous woman’s case tells you that the camp’s management or the organisation she reported to handled it badly—punishing the survivor instead of the perpetrator. That’s a failure of the system, not a reason you should have to stay silent forever. But it does mean you’re right to be cautious.

A well-functioning protection system should **never** move the reporter to a worse location as a solution. The perpetrator should be the one relocated, warned, or restricted. Sometimes camp authorities move the survivor “for her own safety” as a quick fix, but that’s not best practice, and many NGOs now push back against it. So one of your key questions to any potential helper is: *“If I talk to you, will I be forced to move? Has that happened to anyone recently?”*

---

### You matter. Your children matter. Your place matters.
You’ve already shown incredible resourcefulness by adapting your routine. Please hold onto this: **what is happening is not your fault, and you are not “causing trouble” by wanting to live without fear.** The man’s behaviour is the problem, not your reaction to it.

If you want to explore any of these steps more concretely—like how to find out if there’s a confidential hotline, or what to say to a caseworker without giving your name—I can help you think through the exact words. Just let me know what feels most possible right now.
